text: on the use of fluorouracil, and has been shown to produce modest survival benefits.22 Adding folinic acid improves the effi- cacy,23 and the combination has long been regarded as standard. Although it has been suggested that regimens based on continuous infusion of fluorouracil are more ef- fective than those using bolus dosage,2,24 others consider that although response rates are improved, median surviv- al is similar, and that differences in toxicity and conven- ience of administration are more significant in making the choice.20 Oral fluorouracil prodrugs such as capecitabine, or tegafur with uracil, are considered a valid alternative to intravenous fluorouracil.3,25,26 Several newer drugs have now been shown to improve re- sponse rates and survival when used for chemotherapy in these patients. In particular, regimens including irinotecan or oxaliplatin, such as FOLFIRI or FOLFOX, are now considered options for first-line management of metastatic colorectal cancer.3-5,11,27,28 There is also evidence for both improved response and survival when bevacizumab (an antagonist of vascular endothelial growth factor) is added to chemotherapy.29-31 Similarly, cetuximab, a blocker of the epidermal growth factor receptor, appears to improve response rate and decrease the rate of progression if given with irinotecan,32 and preliminary results suggest that it is effective when combined with a FOLFOX regimen.28 US guidelines currently recommend combining bevacizumab with one of the first-line regimens—FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, a fluorouracil/folinic acid regimen, or Cape Ox (capecitab- ine plus oxaliplatin)—in patients with metastatic disease who are able to tolerate intensive therapy,4,5 although the data to support some of these combinations are not yet available. An alternative regimen (without the bevacizum- ab), or cetuximab plus irinotecan, or monotherapy with a drug not included in the original regimen (such as irinote- can, cetuximab, or panitumumab), may be tried in those who fail to respond. Capecitabine, or fluorouracil/folinic acid with or without bevacizumab, are options in those unable to tolerate the more intensive regimens.4,5,11 Other drugs and regimens continue to be investigated. Im- munological therapies under investigation include mono- clonal antibodies, and vaccination with autologous tumour cells or against tumour-associated antigens; gene therapy is another area of research.33 1.
